articles.title: From Document Classification to Scholar Shortlists: An Audit of Shortlist Sensitivity to OpenAlex's Topic-Classifier Update
articles.abstract: Open databases assign topics to works; their case rests on work-level agreement, institutional mix and citation-impact ranking. A list of people adds an ordering rule and a cutoff; none of the three checks covers an author profile or a fixed-length list. In October 2026 OpenAlex replaced its topic assignment. We scored a frozen set under both assignments, holding works, authors, pool and cutoff fixed and re-estimating weights per label world. At work level, 47.0% of 429,985 works changed their primary topic. In top-50 lists we build for six keyword-defined query domains, 80 of 300 seats changed hands (26.7%), 18% to 42% by domain. Across the two specifications built from the archived label tables (B, C) the pooled figure stays between 23.7% and 26.7%; a crossed bracket (D) gives 24.7%, a counting variant (E) 23.3%, and a separate endpoint bracket (A), read on 16 October, 29.3%; three to eight of each top ten kept their seats. Pooled, 42 of the 80 dropped seats fall outside the narrow band, so enrichment at the cut is partial; shorter lists turn over faster. Labels, text and weights moved together, so this is an association between two versions of one database, not an isolated classifier effect. For research evaluation, the question is whether the list, at its length, still names the same people. A shortlist is a reading of one label version at one length; its stability is separate from label accuracy. We state what it should report: the label version, the date it was scored, the length, and the width of the cutoff band.

articles_hidden.title: Paper I: A Funder-Driven Registered Report Initiative Compared with Standard Applications: A Study on Research Quality
articles_hidden.authors: Sigrid Hegna Ingvaldsen; Ida Svege; Jan-Ole Hesselberg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aim: A registered report (RR) commits researchers to a peer-reviewed protocol before results are known, reducing reporting bias and promoting open science. Foundation Dam, a health research funder, launched a two-year initiative incentivising RR applications. This study describes projects choosing RR versus standard applications (SA) and assesses differences in reviewer scores.

Method: The sample comprises all research grant applicants at Foundation Dam, 2023 to 2025 (N=1194). Using a multilevel linear regression model, we compared Excellence and Implementation scores between RR and SA applications across the 2023 research call (SA n=358) with those from the 2024/2025 calls (RR n=142, SA n=694). Intraclass correlation coefficients assessed reviewer-related variance, and exploratory analyses examined reviewers' confidence and disagreement levels. 

Preregistered Stage 1 protocol: https://osf.io/jq84x/overview (date of in-principle acceptance: 20/01/2026).

Results: RR applications were not scored significantly higher than SA applications on Excellence (β= −0.08, 95% CI [−0.20, 0.03], p=.131) or Implementation (β= −0.04, 95% CI [−0.14, 0.06], p=.408). Excellence scores were slightly lower in the 2024/2025 calls than in the 2023 call (β= −0.08, 95% CI [−0.16, 0.00], p=.048), whereas Implementation scores did not change. Reviewer variability accounted for 18.3% of the variance in Excellence scores and 15.4% in Implementation scores, and was not greater for RR than SA applications. 

Conclusion: Findings do not support that choosing RR format yields higher assessed research quality at the application stage, but are informative for funders and journals developing their own RR models.

articles_hidden.title: Gate the claim, not the tool: verification for AI-accelerated research in nutrition
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) and agentic workflows can accelerate nutrition science across living systematic reviews, dietary assessment and cohort analyses, yet they have also fuelled a surge of formulaic papers mined from open datasets. Journals and funders have responded largely by restricting how AI may be used, especially in writing. Because AI use leaves no reliable trace in a single paper, such rules cannot be enforced; they drive use out of sight, penalize honest authors who disclose it, and fall out of date within months as models improve. A gate works only when what it checks is visible at submission. When three publishers stopped accepting unvalidated papers built on the US National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES), their NHANES publications fell by 72% in the first nine months of 2026, showing that visible gates work, though a rule that blunt can also turn away sound epidemiology. Rather than policing the tool, nutrition science should use AI openly under human scientific judgement and hold every result to four verification gates scaled to its consequence: depositing data, code and agent logs so others can rerun the work; naming an accountable investigator who understands the study design and answers for each claim made; independently verifying findings that could change clinical practice or dietary policy; and disclosing what AI and humans did without penalty. As output grows, papers will likely become concise accounts for human readers resting on machine-auditable records, shifting prestige from the journal name to whether a claim matters when verified.
